clue.text: Political philosopher worries about Republican group causing riot?

indicators.note: to be about something is to stand around it, so one piece encircles another

blocks.note: Karl Marx, the political philosopher behind communism
to worry someone is to bother them
R is the standard abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: A thinker frets about a band of Republicans stirring up unrest in the streets.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sets up Marx and politics, so 'riot' reads as civil disorder; it is really a riot of laughter.
explanation.definitionFit: The comedy family of film stars were famously chaotic, and a hilarious performer is colloquially called a riot.

clue.text: Male said to be affected in unusual way?

definitions.text: Male said to be affected in unusual way?

indicators.note: something affected is altered or put on, so the letters take a different form

blocks.note: M is the standard abbreviation for male
taken as written

explanation.surface: Gossip about a man who has reportedly taken something rather strangely.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the definition: legend says this king was cursed with a golden touch, and later given donkey's ears.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth this Phrygian king is famous for a curse that turned his food and his daughter into gold.

clue.text: Cue after grabbing a rest

indicators.note: once something has grabbed another thing it holds it inside

blocks.note: a cue is a prompt or reminder
taken as written

explanation.surface: A snooker or theatre instruction: pick up a breather once your cue comes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cue' tempts you towards snooker or the theatre, but it is a prompt, and 'rest' is the leftover part, not a break.
explanation.definitionFit: What is left over after the rest has been taken away is a remainder; both nouns mean the leftover part.

clue.text: Humber Mud, a short story involving items found on the beach?

indicators.note: something involving another thing includes it within itself, so the letters lie inside the phrase

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word through the start of the last

explanation.surface: A title for a tale about the muddy estuary of the Humber, featuring things washed up on the shore.
explanation.walkthrough: The Humber is a muddy estuary in northern England, which makes the surface plausible; the answer runs from inside 'Humber' to the S of 'story'.
explanation.definitionFit: Knee-length casual trousers are typical holiday wear, so they are seen on the sand; the question mark flags the loose definition.

clue.text: Take possession of old trophy in 100 years

indicators.note: a thing placed in something else sits inside its letters

blocks.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
a cup is a sports trophy
Y is the abbreviation for years

explanation.surface: Finally getting hold of an ancient trophy for the first time in a century.
explanation.walkthrough: '100 years' splits into two separate abbreviations, which wrap around the trophy.
explanation.definitionFit: To occupy territory or a building is to seize and hold it, so the verb phrase is a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: A noted problem solver, I procure hotel undergoing refurbishment

indicators.note: refurbishment rearranges and remakes a place, so these letters are reworked

blocks.note: taken as written, thirteen letters of fodder

explanation.surface: A celebrated fixer boasts of acquiring a hotel that is being done up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Problem solver' suggests a business troubleshooter buying property, but it means a fictional detective.
explanation.definitionFit: Agatha Christie's Belgian sleuth is one of the most famous fictional detectives, solving murder mysteries with his little grey cells.

clue.text: Pack interior of streetcars

indicators.note: the interior is everything except the outside, so only the inner letters are kept

blocks.note: streetcars are TRAMS, whose inside letters are kept

explanation.surface: Commuters squeezed tightly into the inside of city trams.
explanation.walkthrough: Don't look inside the printed word: first turn streetcars into the British word for them, then take its inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To pack something is to cram or force it tightly in, which is the verb sense here.

clue.text: Shelf on which sits small toboggan

indicators.note: in a down entry, what sits on something is written above it

blocks.note: S is the standard abbreviation for small
a ledge is a narrow shelf

explanation.surface: A little toy sledge kept on a shelf.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer the piece that sits on another is written above it.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words name a sled used to slide down snowy slopes, so they are simple synonyms.

clue.text: Object — one associated with Hull — pocketed by doctor

indicators.note: something pocketed is tucked away inside another thing

blocks.note: DR is the abbreviation for doctor
Emu was the puppet bird of British entertainer Rod Hull

explanation.surface: Something from the city of Hull being slipped into a medic's pocket.
explanation.walkthrough: Hull looks like the English port city, but it is Rod Hull, a 1970s-80s British TV comic famous for his aggressive Emu puppet.
explanation.definitionFit: To demur is to raise an objection or express reluctance, so it matches the verb sense of object.

clue.text: Brownish vehicle male crashed

indicators.note: a crashed thing is smashed out of shape, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: a car is a vehicle
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man has wrecked a brown car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brownish' looks like a description of the vehicle, but it is the definition, a colour adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Caramel is a light golden-brown colour, named after cooked sugar, so it describes a brownish shade.

clue.text: Facility with £50 off winter sport equipment

indicators.note: taking something off removes it from what remains

blocks.note: a facility for something is a skill at it
L is the pound sign and also the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A shop offering a fifty-pound discount on skiing gear.
explanation.walkthrough: '£50' looks like one price but supplies two L's: one for the pound, one for fifty.
explanation.definitionFit: A ski is the long runner strapped to each boot for gliding over snow, a piece of cold-season sporting kit.

clue.text: Disconnected and receiving no publicity

blocks.note: first meaning: removed from the electrical socket
second meaning: not promoted, since to plug is to advertise

explanation.surface: Someone cut off from the world and getting no media attention.
explanation.walkthrough: To plug a product is to give it publicity, so the second meaning is a playful literal reading.
explanation.definitionFit: An appliance pulled from its socket is cut off, while an unadvertised show has had no promotional mentions.

clue.text: Where the residents have been spirited away?

definitions.text: Where the residents have been spirited away?

blocks.clueFragment: Where the residents have been spirited away?
blocks.note: surface reading: a place whose people have been whisked off mysteriously
setter's reading: a deserted settlement, with spirits hinting at phantoms

explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirited away' means removed secretly, but spirits are also phantoms, which points to the name for a deserted settlement.
explanation.definitionFit: An abandoned settlement whose inhabitants have all left is commonly described with this phrase.

clue.text: Hey! Ad break periodically censored some stars

indicators.note: cutting at regular intervals removes every other letter, leaving the rest

blocks.note: odd-position letters kept

explanation.surface: A TV broadcaster bleeps out a celebrity's exclamation during a commercial break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stars' suggests celebrities on television, but it means a constellation.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the largest constellation in the sky, named after the many-headed serpent of Greek myth, so a group of stars.

clue.text: Detective Bjorn interrupts brief vacation

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break into the middle of something

blocks.note: hols is British shorthand for holidays
Bjorn is the setter, who refers to himself

explanation.surface: A sleuth named Bjorn barges in on someone's short break.
explanation.walkthrough: Bjorn is the setter of this puzzle, so his name stands for ME; 'brief' signals the clipped British form of holidays.
explanation.definitionFit: Sherlock, Conan Doyle's consulting sleuth of Baker Street, is the archetypal fictional investigator.

clue.text: Very exposed lines become worn down

indicators.note: something exposed has had its covering stripped off, so its outer letters go

blocks.note: the word with first and last letters removed
an ode is a poem, made of lines of verse

explanation.surface: Lines of rock left highly exposed to the weather wear away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very exposed' reads as 'highly exposed', but 'exposed' acts on the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Rock or soil that erodes is gradually worn away by wind and water, matching the intransitive verb phrase.

clue.text: Mark bored by Liberal, a notorious hard-liner

indicators.note: something bored by another has had a hole drilled into it, so a piece goes inside

blocks.note: a stain is a mark
L is the abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: A man named Mark is tired of a dull Liberal politician who turns out to be an extremist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bored' looks like weariness and 'Mark' like a name; it is a stain drilled into.
explanation.definitionFit: The Soviet dictator was infamous for brutal, uncompromising rule, the epitome of an authoritarian zealot.

clue.text: Got lather worked up somewhat slowly

indicators.note: something worked up is agitated and stirred, so the letters are mixed

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone gradually builds up a foam of soap.
explanation.walkthrough: The musical term is a diminutive of largo, so it means fairly slow rather than very slow.
explanation.definitionFit: This Italian tempo marking tells players to perform rather slowly, a little faster than largo.

clue.text: Drink Strega on a regular basis

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is taken

blocks.note: even-position letters kept

explanation.surface: Advice to drink an Italian liqueur habitually.
explanation.walkthrough: Strega is an Italian herbal liqueur, which makes 'Drink' look like an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: The brewed leaf infusion is a common beverage, so it is simply a kind of drink.

clue.text: Easily walk miles in Italian island heading north

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits inside its letters
in a down entry, going north means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: Elba is the Italian island where Napoleon was exiled
M is the abbreviation for miles

explanation.surface: Strolling for miles across an Italian island, heading northward.
explanation.walkthrough: Elba is where Napoleon was first exiled; the island is turned upward with the M already inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To amble is to stroll at a leisurely pace, walking without effort or hurry.

clue.text: Grip end of broken halter awkwardly

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, the only one kept
done awkwardly means clumsily and out of order, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: final letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: Clumsily grabbing the end of a snapped horse's harness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grip' looks like part of the horse-handling picture, but it is the definition in its sense of captivate.
explanation.definitionFit: A gripping story holds your attention completely, which is what it means to enthral an audience.

clue.text: Pitch starts to turn at Rawalpindi

indicators.note: starts are opening letters, so only the first of each word is kept

blocks.note: initial letters

explanation.surface: A cricket pitch in Pakistan begins to take spin.
explanation.walkthrough: Rawalpindi is a Pakistani Test cricket venue, and a turning pitch helps spin bowlers; but pitch here is the black sticky substance.
explanation.definitionFit: Pitch is a dark resinous substance like the bitumen used on roads, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Angular figure seen in velour homburg

indicators.note: something seen in a phrase is visible inside it, sitting among its letters

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: A geometric pattern on a soft felt hat.
explanation.walkthrough: A homburg is a felt hat with a dented crown, and velour is a plush fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an older name for a rhombus, a four-sided shape with equal sides and slanted corners.

clue.text: Spenser tenet reworked into part of speech

indicators.note: something reworked has been redone in a new form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A belief of the poet Edmund Spenser gets turned into a grammar lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: Edmund Spenser was the Elizabethan poet of The Faerie Queene; 'part of speech' is loose here, as this is a verb form rather than a word class.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the grammatical verb form for actions happening now, a component of how we use language.
